summary: Defines MIB objects for monitoring and controlling network devices that provide APPN Extended Border Node capabilities. It supports managing connections between APPN networks. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a set of gauges for the gateway machines that connect separate older IBM networks, so a manager can watch how they are doing.

what is an extended border node
what is an appn subnet routing list
subtitle: SNMP objects for watching how Extended Border Nodes split APPN networks into subnets and route sessions between them.

tldr.problem: Extended Border Nodes partition an APPN network into subnets, which makes it hard for customers to see the end-to-end route of a session across subnet boundaries or how directory searches are controlled between subnets.
tldr.mechanism: The EBN MIB adds tables that extend the APPN MIB: subnet affiliation of LUs, the route and class of service on the far side of the EBN, COS mappings, the subnet routing list, and HPR session identifiers.
tldr.outcome: Managers can monitor EBN behavior, but the module does not configure EBN nodes and defines no traps. It is a Proposed Standard from November 1998 and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 2457 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1998. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends tables of the APPN MIB in RFC 2455.

sections.title: Purpose and Framework
sections.content:
RFC 2457 is a product of the SNA NAU Services MIB Working Group. It defines a MIB module for managing devices with APPN Extended Border Node (EBN) capabilities. The module is SMIv2 and uses the key words of RFC 2119.

It sits inside the SNMP Network Management Framework: the architecture of RFC 2271, the SMI, MIB-II, the SNMP protocol, the user-based security model and the view-based access control model. The Framework permits new objects to be defined for experimentation and evaluation.
sections.plainLanguage: This document lists the dials and gauges that a special gateway machine in an old IBM network can show to its manager.

sections.title: Why Border Nodes Need Monitoring
sections.content:
In a single APPN network all topology information goes to all network nodes (NNs), and directory searches can be forwarded to all of them. As the network grows this traffic could become prohibitive, and enterprises joined through APPN may want to be shielded from each other's traffic. An EBN lets customers partition the network into subnets.

An EBN blocks topology exchange between subnets and controls where directory searches are forwarded. A subnetwork is a cluster of NNs sharing the same topology. A boundary occurs where an EBN and an adjacent NN have different network identifiers (NETIDs), or the same NETID but a configured boundary. The link at a boundary is an Intersubnetwork Transmission Group (ISTG). The EBN's own subnet is its native subnetwork; the other is non-native.

The cost is that customers may struggle to determine the end-to-end route of sessions that cross boundaries, and to understand how directory searches are controlled. This MIB addresses those issues.
sections.plainLanguage: A big town can get too noisy, so it is split into neighborhoods with a gatekeeper at each border. This MIB lets the manager see what the gatekeepers are doing.

sections.title: Structure of the Module
sections.content:
The module extends tables of the SNANAU APPN MIB (RFC 2455). Its six groups are:

  • ebnDir: subnet information about LUs, an extension of appnDirTable. The value of ebnDirSubnetAffiliation is native(1), nonNative(2) or subarea(3).
  • ebnIsRscv: the Route Selection Control Vector (RSCV) and class of service (COS) toward the BIND destination, an extension of appnIsInTable.
  • ebnDirConfig: directory caching and the default maximum number of subnetworks a LOCATE search may traverse.
  • ebnCos: COS mapping between subnetworks.
  • ebnSubnetRoutingList: the customer-supplied list of where to forward search requests.
  • hbn: High Performance Routing (HPR) EBN intermediate session information.

The module does not support configuration of EBN nodes, historical information about session initiation failures, or Peripheral Border Node (PBN) support. It defines no traps either; the APPN MIB's alert trap may carry a pointer to an object from this MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: The module is a binder with six tabs. Each tab answers one kind of question about the border gatekeeper.

sections.title: Session Routes and Class of Service
sections.content:
The APPN MIB's appnIsInTable can hold the RSCV and COS name for only one subnetwork a session crosses. ebnIsRscvTable adds the other one. When an EBN changes the RSCV before forwarding a BIND, appnIsInRouteInfo holds the incoming RSCV and ebnIsRscvDestinationRoute holds the outgoing one.

The RFC walks through three cases with a primary logical unit (PLU, the initiator) and a secondary logical unit (SLU, the destination). With EBN1 connected to EBN2, appnIsInRouteInfo at EBN1 is the route from the PLU to EBN2 and ebnIsRscvDestinationRoute is the one-hop route to EBN2. With an EBN connected to an NN or PBN, the SLU must be in the second subnet. With an NN or PBN connected to an EBN, the PLU must be in the first subnet.

For class of service, ebnIsRscvDestinationCos at an EBN is the COS used toward the SLU. The ebnCosMapTable shows how non-native COS values are mapped to native ones. It reports the mappings the EBN is actually performing, not the user-defined initial mappings.
sections.plainLanguage: When a letter crosses a border, the route and the delivery speed on the far side can differ from the near side. These tables record both, so the manager can follow the whole trip.

sections.title: Subnet Search Lists
sections.content:
The subnet routing list says to which adjacent nodes an EBN forwards LOCATE search requests. ebnSubnetSearchTable has an entry for each LU name with a defined list. The name may be a single LU, a partial wildcard (a name prefix followed by an asterisk), or a full wildcard (a single asterisk). Its objects say whether the EBN may add dynamic entries (none, limited or full) and whether entries may be reordered (priority or defined).

ebnSearchTable lists, in configured order, each control point name to search for an LU name. Besides normal names and wildcards, the special name SELF (with a leading asterisk) means the EBN searches itself and its native subnetwork at that point, and the special name EBNS (with a leading asterisk) means all native EBNs. The tables show only the configured list; the order of an actual search is worked out dynamically by the EBN.

Directory settings include ebnSearchCacheTime in minutes and ebnMaxSearchCache in entries; a value of 0 means no defined limit.
sections.plainLanguage: When the gatekeeper has to find someone, it follows a list of neighborhoods to ask. The list says who to ask and in what order.

sections.title: Compliance and HPR Sessions
sections.content:
The hbnIsInTable extends appnIsInTable for sessions routed between back-to-back Rapid Transport Protocol (RTP) connections in an HPR EBN. It gives the network connection endpoint identifier (NCE ID) and transport connection identifier (TCID) for the second RTP connection, toward the SLU.

The compliance statement ebnCompliance makes five groups unconditionally mandatory: directory, intermediate session RSCV, directory configuration, COS mapping and subnet routing list. The hbnIsInGroup is mandatory only for HPR extended border nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every border machine must offer the main five tabs of the binder. Only machines of the special fast kind must offer the sixth.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some of the management information may be sensitive in some environments, so authentication of SNMP requests and controlled access SHOULD be used there. None of the read-only objects reports a password, user data or anything particularly sensitive, but enterprises that regard their network configuration, usage and performance as corporate assets may want to restrict access to most objects.

There are no read-write objects in the EBN MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: The gauges only let you look, never change anything, but a company may still want to limit who gets to look.
